title: GEESE
subtitle: The band from New York.
articleTitle: RUIDO PARA UNA CIUDAD QUE NO DUERME
author: Por Vera Ledesma
paragraphs: En un subsuelo de Brooklyn, mientras el tren retumba bajo el piso y una lámpara insiste en parpadear, Geese afina como si estuviera armando una máquina. Cada instrumento avanza en una dirección diferente, pero el choque termina formando una sola criatura: nerviosa, imprevisible y extrañamente precisa.
La banda creció entre salas de ensayo prestadas, cables enredados y conciertos donde la mitad del público todavía no sabía qué estaba escuchando. Esa incertidumbre se volvió parte de su lenguaje.

"Nos interesa el momento en que una canción casi se rompe", dice uno de sus integrantes en esta entrevista imaginaria. No habla de caos gratuito, sino de tensión: tocar lo suficientemente cerca del borde como para que cada decisión importe.

Nueva York aparece en su música sin necesidad de ser nombrada. Está en la urgencia, en las capas que compiten por espacio y en la sensación de que algo distinto puede ocurrir al doblar cualquier esquina.

Antes de irnos, vuelven a tocar el mismo fragmento. Esta vez dura menos de un minuto y suena completamente distinto. Quizás ahí esté la clave: para Geese, una canción no es un destino fijo, sino una pregunta que cambia cada vez que alguien intenta responderla.
note: Este reportaje es una pieza editorial ficticia creada para ARE WE THERE YET?

title: WHERE ARE WE?
author: elias grau
paragraphs: David Lynch rarely needed a monster - A hallway was enough. A staircase. A motel room. A curtain. An empty road illuminated by headlights. A living room that feels perfectly normal until somebody remains silent for two seconds longer than they should. Lynch understood something that architecture usually tries to hide: spaces are not neutral.

A corridor exists because you are supposed to leave one place and arrive somewhere else. A hotel room belongs to you, but only temporarily. A waiting room is designed around an event that has not happened yet. A highway at night is neither origin nor destination.

These are transitional spaces. They are supposed to disappear while we use them. Lynch makes us stay. Think about the Red Room in Twin Peaks. It resembles a room, but almost everything inside it rejects the logic of an ordinary room. The curtains suggest a stage without revealing what is behind them. The floor produces an aggressive geometry. There appears to be no obvious entrance or exit.
It is interior architecture without an exterior. You could almost describe it as a waiting room for reality. The same unease appears elsewhere.

The corridors of the Lost Highway Hotel. The anonymous rooms of Mulholland Drive. The industrial spaces surrounding Eraserhead. Roads emerging from darkness without showing where they began. Lynch repeatedly places characters in environments that appear recognizable while withholding the information that normally makes a place understandable.
Where are we? How did we enter? What happens behind that door? Why is nobody else here?

This is close to what we now call a liminal space: an environment defined less by what it is than by the fact that it sits between two states. Academic work on Lynch has similarly examined how interiors, color and spatial ambiguity become part of his visual narrative rather than mere backgrounds.
But there is an important difference between a random photograph of an empty shopping mall and a Lynchian room.

The empty mall is unsettling because nobody is there. Lynch is unsettling because it feels like somebody was there. Or will be. The room contains expectation. This is why his spaces often feel dreamlike without looking completely fantastical. Dreams rarely invent architecture from nothing. They misuse architecture we already know.

Your school becomes your grandmother's house. A bedroom opens into a restaurant. A hallway becomes longer than the building containing it. We accept the impossible floor plan because the individual pieces are familiar. Lynch worked the same way. He didn't need to invent another planet. He only needed to move the door.
